1:
The chapter opens with a prophet suddenly seized by the Spirit, and the witnesses gather first around his shadowy identity and then around the errand that inspiration set him. The reformed John Gill notes that some, following Hillerus, take Azariah the son of Oded to be the very same as Iddo, and that the Jews reckoned him the prophet once sent to reprove Jeroboam for the altar he had built; the Targum, Gill adds, reads that "the spirit of prophecy" came upon him, instructing him what to say to Asa. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the Hebrew more starkly — "and Azariah son of Oded, there fell upon him spirit of God," a holy inspiration — yet confesses the prophet is otherwise unknown: the name Oded comprises the same radical letters as Iddo, named at 2 Chron. 9:29 and 12:15, but whether the same man or another is meant lies beyond decision. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke says as much in a sentence: we know nothing of this prophet but what is related of him here.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lifts the bare notice into a meditation on the mercy of a preaching ministry. It was a great happiness to Israel, he says, that they had prophets among them, even while they remained strangely addicted to idolatry; for the scriptures are of all the surest word of prophecy, and a church cannot be so easily imposed upon by a counterfeit Bible as by a counterfeit prophet. Here a prophet is sent to Asa and his army as they return victorious from the war with the Ethiopians at 2 Chron. 14:9 — not to compliment them on their success but to quicken them to their duty, which Henry calls the proper business of God's ministers even with princes and the greatest of men.

On the descent of the Spirit itself the two schools speak with one voice. Henry reads it as a double endowment — the Spirit came upon the prophet both to instruct him what he should say and to enable him to say it with clearness and boldness; and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley compresses the same thought into a line, that the Spirit came both to instruct him what to say and to enable him to say it plainly and boldly. So the witnesses set the frame for the whole chapter. An unknown man, filled from heaven, meets a king flushed with victory and turns the hour of triumph into a summons to perseverance — proof, before a word of the sermon is heard, that God's richest gift to a wavering people is a faithful voice that will tell them the truth.
2:
The prophet meets the returning king before the gates and preaches a sermon compressed into a single covenantal maxim. The reformed John Gill sets the scene simply: Azariah went out from Jerusalem to meet Asa as he was coming to it. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms that the prophet met the king on his return from battle, and hears in the opening address, "Hear ye me, Asa, and all Judah," a deliberate echo of Abijah's speech to the northern tribes at 2 Chron. 13:4. The core sentence — "The LORD is with you, while ye be with him" — Ellicott would render as a backward glance at the recent victory: Jehovah was with you in the battle because ye were with him, clinging to him for help, as Asa had done at 2 Chron. 14:11. He calls the sequel, "if ye seek him, he will be found of you; but if ye forsake him, he will forsake you," a favourite formula of the chronicler, drawn from David's charge at 1 Chron. 28:9 and echoed at Jeremiah 29:13.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fastens on the double clause as the settled and eternal purpose of God: to those who seek him he will ever be found propitious, and them alone will he abandon who forsake him. In this verse, Clarke insists, the unconditional perseverance of the saints has no place — a doctrine he traces back to the serpent's first lie, "ye shall not die," and calls the plague and disgrace of the church ever since. He quotes the Targum's paraphrase with delight: the Word of the LORD shall be your helper while ye walk in his ways; if ye seek doctrine from his presence he will be found of you in times of trouble, but if ye cast away his fear he will abandon you.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the maxim as at once comfort and caution. It is comfort, that those who keep close to God shall always have his presence with them; but it is caution too, for he is with them no longer than they are with him — the signal favour just shown in the field is no freehold, but a tenancy that hangs upon their perseverance. Henry presses the promise "if you seek him he will be found of you" against the pledge of Heb. 11:6, that God is the rewarder of them that diligently seek him, and never said to any, Seek ye me in vain. The witnesses converge: Asa is put on his good behaviour, and the whole reformation to follow is the king's answer to a word that made his triumph conditional on his fidelity.
3:
To illustrate his maxim the prophet points to Israel's long seasons "without the true God, and without a teaching priest, and without law" — and here the witnesses openly divide over the time the words describe. The reformed John Gill observes that the period is left unexpressed, whether past, present, or to come; the Targum refers it to the separation of the ten tribes and the calf-worship of Jeroboam, while others read it of the future, fulfilled in the Babylonish captivity. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke weighs the same options and settles for the recent past: some make it a prophecy of the final ruin of the Jews, others refer it to the state of the people under Rehoboam and Abijah, which was happily changed under Asa — and this, he says, appears the most natural sense. John Wesley, of the same school, casts it further back still, understanding Israel of the whole nation in former times, and especially in the days of the Judges, when they were often without the settled knowledge and worship of the true God and without teaching priests, as the book of Judges plainly shows.

The grammatical-historical witnesses resist pinning the words to any single era. Keil and Delitzsch insist we must supply neither a preterite nor a future but read the present — "Many days is Israel without the true God" — taking the phrase in a general sense that Israel had already tasted in the time of the Judges yet would taste far more deeply in the future, under the idolatrous kings and in the Assyrian and Babylonian exile; they find the future reference confirmed by Hosea, who at Hosea 3:4 threatens the ten tribes with just such a condition. Charles Ellicott likewise calls the verse an illustration of the general truth of the previous verse, adducing the periods of decline recorded in the book of Judges at Judges 2:11 and since the division of the kingdom as historical proof; the "teaching priest" he grounds in the law's charge at Lev. 10:11 and Malachi 2:7, and "the true God" in Jeremiah 10:10.

So the debate is genuine and threefold: does the prophet look back to the anarchy of the Judges, sideways to the recent apostasy of the northern tribes, or forward to a desolation still to come? The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lays all three readings side by side without forcing a verdict, content that whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our admonition — for on any reading the lesson stands, that a people who forsake teaching, priest, and law are left defenceless, and that God is with them only while they are with him.
4:
Against that dark backdrop of desolation the prophet sets a bright and recurring turn: "but when they in their trouble did turn unto the LORD... and sought him, he was found of them." The reformed John Gill reads the whole movement of repentance — when Israel were carried captive by their neighbours and oppressed, they cried unto the LORD, repented of their sins, turned from them to him, and were heard. The trouble was the schoolmaster that drove them home; the turning was real, an abandonment of the very sins that had provoked the judgment.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the Hebrew and the pattern. The verse reads literally, "and he returned in his straits unto Jehovah, the God of Israel; they sought him," the singular yielding at once to the plural as the nation is gathered into one penitent. The language of returning "in straits" he ties to the promise of Deut. 4:30, that when thou art in tribulation, if thou turn to the LORD and be obedient unto his voice, he will not forsake thee; and the recurring cycle of oppression and deliverance he documents from the book of Judges, at Judges 3:9 and following, and from the psalmist's confession at Ps. 106:44, that God regarded their affliction when he heard their cry. The verse is thus the hinge of the prophet's argument — the same God who withdrew when they forsook him is found the moment they seek him again.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the encouragement out plainly: when their troubles drove them to God, they found it not in vain to seek him. Here is the maxim of the second verse turned into history and made a ground of hope. However often Israel had broken with God, they never found him unwilling to be reconciled; the door that their apostasy had shut, their repentance found open. Henry will not let the mercy dissolve the justice — the turning had to be genuine, a returning to duty and not merely a cry under the lash — but he insists the record is set down to invite even backsliders home. The three witnesses converge on a single evangelical note. Gill fixes the reality of the repentance, Ellicott the grammar and the biblical pattern of the cycle, Henry the comfort that flows from it: that a people is never so far gone in trouble that seeking God is a wasted labour, for the promise "he was found of them" has behind it the whole history of a nation forgiven again and again.
5:
The sermon now pictures the wretchedness of the godless seasons in concrete terms — "in those times there was no peace to him that went out, nor to him that came in, but great vexations were upon all the inhabitants of the countries." The reformed John Gill reads it of the collapse of ordinary life: there was no safety for travellers going abroad from one part to another about their trade and business, the highways being infested with thieves and robbers. Apostasy, in his reading, unravels the common security of a nation until a man cannot walk the roads in peace.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott anchors "those times" to the "many days" of the third verse, the seasons of national unfaithfulness, and refines the vocabulary. The picture of no peace to goer-out or comer-in he traces to the desolation of Judges 5:6, when the highways were unoccupied and travellers walked through byways; and "great vexations" he renders "great confusions," the Hebrew word foretold as a punishment of apostasy at Deut. 28:20 and used of tumults at Amos 3:9, "the countries" being the territories or provinces of Israel. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the verse to the same effect — when Israel lived in the gross neglect of God and his law, men could not go abroad about their private occasions without great danger, as it was in the days of Shamgar at Judges 5:6.

Adam Clarke, of the same school, lifts his eyes from the ancient scene to a greater one, asking whether our Lord did not allude to this verse and the next when he foretold wars and rumours of wars, nation rising against nation and kingdom against kingdom, at Matt. 24:6-7. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the whole into his portrait of the forsaken nation, continually embarrassed with vexatious and destroying wars, foreign and domestic, and harassed by one enemy after another until they were vexed with all adversity. The witnesses do not divide; each unfolds a facet of the same ruin. Gill fixes the plundered highways, Ellicott and Wesley the biblical echoes of the Judges and the covenant curse, Clarke the prophetic reach of the words into the discourse of Christ, and Henry the moral: that when a people provoke God with all iniquity, he vexes them with all adversity, and the peace that departs with faith does not return until faith does.
6:
The desolation reaches its climax in mutual destruction — "and nation was destroyed of nation, and city of city: for God did vex them with all adversity" — and the witnesses read it as the self-consuming fury of a people abandoned by God to itself. The reformed John Gill takes "nation" of the tribes turned upon one another: one tribe destroyed by another, as the Ephraimites by the Gileadites, and the tribe of Benjamin by the rest, and Shechem by Abimelech. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads it identically — one part of the people of Israel destroyed the other by civil wars; for as all Israel is called a nation, so its several tribes are sometimes called nations.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms the sense and enriches it: "they were crushed, nation by nation and city by city," the word "nation" being goy, a community of kindred such as a clan or tribe rather than a mere political mass. The allusion, he says, is to the old feuds between Ephraim and Gilead at Judges 12 and between Benjamin and the other tribes at Judges 20; the internecine strife it paints is like that of Isaiah 19:2, where God sets Egyptian against Egyptian, city against city, kingdom against kingdom. "Did vex them with all adversity" he renders "had confounded them with every kind of distress," comparing the great confusion from the LORD of Zechariah 14:13.

Keil and Delitzsch dwell on the theology of that confounding. The verb, they explain, denotes the confusion which God brings about in order to destroy his enemies, as at the Red Sea in Exodus 14:24 and against the Canaanites at Gibeon; and they press the point that these desolations, already experienced in the defections after Joshua at Judges 2:11, would be tasted still more enduringly in the future, under the idolatrous kings and in the exile, exactly as Hosea threatens the ten tribes at Hosea 3:4. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry seals it with his epigram: they provoked God with all iniquity, and then he vexed them with all adversity. The witnesses do not contend; they render one portrait of a nation whose forsaking of God turned its own strength inward, so that the very brotherhood of the tribes became the instrument of their ruin — a confusion that was not blind chance but the hand of God confounding a people that would not have him rule.
7:
The sermon ends not in lament but in a bracing charge: "Be ye strong therefore, and let not your hands be weak: for your work shall be rewarded." The reformed John Gill takes it as a call to persevere in the reformation already begun — be hearty, earnest, and vigorous, not languid and remiss in reforming the worship of God, which Asa had started to do. The prophet does not merely diagnose the disease of apostasy; he sends the king back to the cure with fresh resolve.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses the wording and calls the verse the moral of the whole address. "Be ye strong therefore" he would render "But ye, be ye strong," the emphatic pronoun setting this generation over against the failed forefathers just described; "let not your hands be weak" is literally, let them not droop or hang down, the same image of failing hands at Zephaniah 3:16 and 2 Samuel 4:1; and "your work shall be rewarded" is, literally, there is indeed a reward for your work, words that recur in the comfort of Jeremiah 31:16. The "work" in view, Ellicott specifies, is the rooting out of idolatry — the conclusion of the prophet's argument being, do not ye fall away like your fathers, but let your allegiance to the LORD be decided and sincere. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads it to the same purpose: go on resolutely to maintain God's worship and to root out idolatry as you have begun, for this is the only method of preserving yourselves from such calamities as your predecessors have felt.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws two lessons from the promised reward. God's work, he notes, should be done with diligence and cheerfulness, yet will not be done without resolution; and the certainty of recompense should quicken us to the work of religion, for we shall be sure not to lose by it in the end. How could it go unrewarded, Henry asks, when the work is its own reward? The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the summons to persevere, Ellicott the emphatic grammar and the cross-references that give the reward its weight, Wesley the practical aim of rooting out idolatry, and Henry the doctrine that God's service, however arduous, never finally impoverishes the servant. The prophet's whole discourse, having traced the ruin of the faithless, closes by handing the faithful king a spade and a promise — dig out the idols, and heaven will see to the wages.
8:
The sermon bears fruit at once: Asa "took courage, and put away the abominable idols... and renewed the altar of the LORD." Yet the verse names the preacher as "Oded the prophet," where the first verse had named "Azariah the son of Oded," and the witnesses divide over the discrepancy. The reformed John Gill reports that some suppose a lost prophecy of Oded the father, but judges rather that Oded here is the son himself, noting that the Vulgate, the Syriac, and the Alexandrian Septuagint all read "Azariah the son of Oded." John Wesley agrees flatly: "of Oded" means of Azariah, who was also called by his father's name Oded. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott finds the Hebrew — "the prophecy Oded the prophet," without any connecting word — suspicious, and suggests that "Oded the prophet" is a marginal gloss crept into the text, or that a lacuna has swallowed the words "which Azariah son of Oded spake"; Keil and Delitzsch likewise call the phrase surprising and record the old conjecture that the words "son of Azariah" dropped out by a copyist's error. So the debate stands: is "Oded" simply Azariah under his father's name, or a corruption in the text?

On the reformation itself the witnesses are warmly agreed. Ellicott renders "he took courage" as "he strengthened himself," the very verb the prophet had used in bidding him be strong at v.7; the "abominable idols" are shiqqutsim, one of Scripture's many terms of contempt for idols, as at 1 Kings 11:5; and the cities taken "from mount Ephraim" he refers to Abijah's conquests at 2 Chron. 13:19, or to towns Asa annexed after his victory over Zerah. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marks the change in the king: his victory had given him some resolution, but this message from God gave him much more, so that now he ventured to destroy all the idols — for all idolatries are abominable, as Peter says at 1 Pet. 4:3 — and to repair an altar already fallen into disuse, though Solomon had built it scarcely sixty years before, so soon do ceremonial institutions begin to wax old and vanish away, as at Heb. 8:13.

Over the "renewing" of the altar a lesser difference appears. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke takes it to mean the altar was dedicated afresh or perhaps enlarged, that more sacrifices might be offered on it than before; Ellicott, following the Septuagint and Vulgate rendering "dedicated," reads a reconsecration of an altar defiled by an illegal worship, though he allows the word may mean no more than repaired. The witnesses leave both threads plainly on view — a textual knot about the prophet's name, and a courage born of preaching that turned a victorious king into a reformer.
9:
The reformation widens into a great assembly, and the witnesses attend to the strangers who swell it — men "out of Ephraim and Manasseh, and out of Simeon" who had fallen to Asa from the northern kingdom. The reformed John Gill glosses them briefly as the proselytes of the gate gathered with Judah and Benjamin. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads their motive: many out of the several tribes, reflecting that the divine blessing was promised to the house of David and finding Jeroboam's government founded in idolatry, would through a spirit of piety leave their own country and go where they might enjoy the worship of the true God.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets this migration among the recurring accessions to the southern kingdom — a like influx under Rehoboam at 2 Chron. 11:16 and another under Hezekiah at 2 Chron. 30:11 — and pauses over the puzzle of Simeon, whose territory lay within Judah's own borders. Perhaps, he suggests, a portion of that tribe had migrated northward, as Genesis 49:7 foretold that Simeon would be scattered in Israel; or perhaps, though politically one with Judah, Simeon was religiously isolated by an illegal worship of its own, though this hardly agrees with the clause "they fell to him out of Israel." The reason for the whole exodus he finds in the words themselves — "when they saw that the LORD his God was with him," for they had heard of Asa's great deliverance from Zerah. Keil and Delitzsch fix the occasion in the fifteenth year of Asa's reign, held soon after the return from the Cushite war, and read the coming festival as the fruit of that victory.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns the accession into a lesson on holy company. It was because they saw that the LORD was with Asa that the strangers came over, and it is good, he says, to be with those who have God with them, to contract acquaintance and friendship with those who live in his fear and favour — for the promise of Zechariah 8:23 is that men shall take hold of the skirt of a Jew, saying, We will go with you, for we have heard that God is with you. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Ellicott identify who came, Clarke and Henry why they came, Keil when they came; and together they show the reformation drawing to itself, as by a magnet, every heart in the divided nation that still longed for the true God — so that Asa's fidelity became a gathering-point for the faithful of tribes not his own.
10:
The assembly convenes "at Jerusalem in the third month, in the fifteenth year of the reign of Asa," and the witnesses linger over the timing and the willingness of those who gathered. The reformed John Gill notes plainly that they came together by the order of Asa, the king having summoned them. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes the season: the third month was the time of the feast of Pentecost, held in that month, so that the sacred convocation likely coincided with one of Israel's great appointed feasts.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the meeting soon after the return from the war against the Cushites, held in the fifteenth year, when they offered of the booty captured from Zerah's host at 2 Chron. 14:14; the sacrifice, they observe, was drawn from the spoil, which suggests the festival followed hard upon the victory. They weigh the chronology with care — the Cushite attack fell in Asa's eleventh year, yet how long the war lasted, and when the king returned to Jerusalem, the text does not say — so that ample room remains for the muster and the feast to fall in the fifteenth. The very fact that the victims were of the captured cattle, they reason, binds the covenant-day closely to the campaign whose plunder supplied it, the one flowing naturally into the other.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry seizes on a fine turn between this verse and the last. The ninth verse had said that Asa gathered them; this verse says that they gathered themselves together — and Henry hears in the difference the readiness of a willing people: so forward were they to obey the king's orders that his command and their own act became one. The meeting was held in the third month, probably at Pentecost, which fell in that month. The witnesses do not divide; each supplies a facet of the same scene. Gill fixes the royal summons, Clarke and Henry the Pentecostal season, Keil the nearness of the feast to the victory and the offering drawn from its spoils. Between them they show a convocation that was at once commanded and embraced — a king calling his people to renew their covenant, and a people running to answer, so that the reformation Asa had begun from above met a devotion rising to meet it from below. The gathering is the visible hinge of the chapter, where the prophet's word, the king's courage, and the people's willingness converge upon a single day at Jerusalem.
11:
The gathered nation opens the day with sacrifice — "they offered unto the LORD the same time, of the spoil which they had brought, seven hundred oxen and seven thousand sheep." The reformed John Gill identifies the spoil precisely: it was brought from the camp of the Ethiopians and the cities of the Philistines, the Targum adding that the offering fell on the feast of weeks, or Pentecost. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke likewise traces the victims to the plunder taken from Zerah and his auxiliaries recorded at 2 Chron. 14:14-15. The offering, in both readings, is a thank-offering carved out of a conquest — the tangible firstfruits of the deliverance God had given.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes the date and the substance. "The same time" means on that day appointed for the festival, in the third month, that is Sivan, corresponding to part of May and June; and the spoil was that of Zerah, the cities round Gerar, and the nomadic tribes overthrown at 2 Chron. 14:13-15. Keil and Delitzsch note that the phrase "they brought of the spoil" defines the sacrifice more closely — they sacrificed, that is, from the booty — and infer that the festival was held soon after the return from the war, the offering being drawn from the very cattle captured in it.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the offering against a greater one and draws out its meaning. These sacrifices were Asa's share of the spoil rendered back to God; yet their number, seven hundred oxen and seven thousand sheep, was nothing to Solomon's vast oblation at the temple's dedication in 2 Chron. 7:5 — a diminution, Henry supposes, owing either to a lessening of their zeal or of their wealth. The victims were meant by way of thanksgiving for the favours they had received and supplication for further favours; and Henry lifts the type into its gospel counterpart, that prayers and praises are now our spiritual sacrifices. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Clarke fix the origin of the spoil, Ellicott the date and the scattered enemies it came from, Keil the nearness of feast to victory, Henry the devotion and the comparison that measures it. Between them they show a people who would not enter into covenant empty-handed, but laid on God's altar the plunder God had given them — turning the wages of war into an act of worship, and the memory of a battle won into a fresh cry for grace to come.
12:
At the heart of the day stands a solemn engagement: "they entered into a covenant to seek the LORD God of their fathers with all their heart and with all their soul." The reformed John Gill records the ancient form the ceremony may have taken, noting with Piscator that they passed between the pieces of a calf cut asunder to ratify the covenant, after the manner of the rite in Jeremiah 34:18. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sets out the covenant in two articles: first, we will seek the God of our fathers with all our heart and soul; second, whosoever, great or small, man or woman, will not worship the true God and serve him alone shall be put to death. Thus no toleration was given to idolatry, and the whole was confirmed with an oath, so that God accepted them and their service.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms the sense and the sources. The phrase means that they bound themselves by an oath, as the next verses show, comparing the covenant of Jeremiah 34:10 and the sworn engagement of Nehemiah 10:29; and "to seek the LORD with all their heart" he traces to the very words of Deut. 4:29, that if thou seek him with all thy heart and soul, thou shalt find him. Keil and Delitzsch read it as a renewal rather than a new thing — they bound themselves by a sworn promise to hold the covenant already theirs, to worship Jahve the God of the fathers with their whole heart and soul.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the pastoral lesson. It is proper for penitents and converts to renew their covenants, and though no vow could lay a higher obligation on them than the divine precept already did, yet the engagement would increase their sense of that obligation, arm them against temptation, and, by joining all together, let them strengthen one another's hands. What is religion, Henry asks, but seeking God, inquiring after him, applying to him upon all occasions? — and they resolved to seek him as the God of their fathers, in the way their fathers sought him, and to do it with all their heart, for only those seek God acceptably who are inward with him and entire for him. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Clarke fix the form and the terms, Ellicott and Keil the biblical roots and the covenant's renewing character, Henry the heart-work it demanded. Between them they show a nation binding itself, by oath and sacrifice, to the very duty it already owed — turning bare obligation into willing devotion, and making its allegiance to God a thing sworn, public, and shared.
13:
The covenant carried a severe sanction: "whosoever would not seek the LORD God of Israel should be put to death, whether small or great, whether man or woman." The reformed John Gill glosses it narrowly — this touched whoever obstinately refused to worship God and served other gods, which by the law was already deserving of death. The clause is not a new invention of Asa's zeal but the enforcement of a standing statute.

The grammatical-historical witnesses agree. Charles Ellicott calls it part of the solemn oath of king and people, a sanction prescribed by the law of Deut. 13:6 and following, and of Deut. 17:2-6. Keil and Delitzsch read it as the proof of their sincerity: to attest the genuineness of their return to the LORD they determined to punish defection from Jahve, on the part of any without respect to age or sex, with death, exactly according to the command in Deut. 17:2-6 — for not to seek Jahve was, in substance, to serve other gods, which that law visited with death by stoning.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the clause with a longer conscience. The people bound themselves to oblige others, to the utmost of their power, to seek God, agreeing that whosoever would not — the man who worshipped other gods, or who obstinately refused to join in the worship of the true God, the settled idolater or the settled atheist — should be put to death; and this, Henry stresses, was no law of their own making but an order to execute the divine precept, which, had it been duly executed before, would have spared the land the abominable idols found in it. Yet Henry raises the question a Christian reader must ask — whether men may now, under the gospel, be compelled by such methods to seek the Lord — and answers with a caution, that the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, though mighty. The witnesses do not divide over the fact: all read the death-sanction as the enforcement of the Mosaic law, not a novelty of Asa's court. Gill and Ellicott fix its legal root, Keil its function as the seal of a sincere return, Henry its rationale and its limit. Between them they show a nation so in earnest with its covenant that it staked life itself on fidelity — a severity proper to the old economy of a theocratic state, which Henry is careful not to transplant unaltered into the age of the gospel, where the sword that guards the truth is not of steel.
14:
The oath was taken not in a whisper but with fanfare: "they sware unto the LORD with a loud voice, and with shouting, and with trumpets, and with cornets." The reformed John Gill reads the loudness as a mark of holy boldness — they were not ashamed of the oath they took, and swore aloud that there might be witnesses of it, and that it might be clear they used no equivocation but expressed themselves in plain words. The very volume was a testimony to the honesty of the vow.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears in the clamour the heightening of a solemn act: the acclamations of the people, accompanied by the loud blasts of trumpet and clarion, naturally enhanced the solemnity of the oath, after the manner of the great musical services described at 1 Chron. 15:28 and 2 Chron. 23:13. Keil and Delitzsch note the single Hebrew word that gathers up the scene — they swore aloud and solemnly, with joyful shouting and the sound of trumpets and horns — and read the whole as the outward sign of an inward gladness, since, as the next verse says, they had sworn with all their heart.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry dwells on the joy that filled the ceremony. They did not swear to God with reluctance, as a poor debtor confesses a judgment to his creditor, but with all the pleasure and satisfaction imaginable, as a bridegroom plights his troth to his bride in the marriage covenant. They swore with a loud voice to express their own zeal and to animate one another, and every honest Israelite was pleased with his own engagement to God and pleased with his neighbour's too. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the boldness of the open oath, Ellicott and Keil the trumpets and shouting that lent it solemnity, Henry the gladness that turned a binding vow into a festival. Between them they portray a covenant sworn in broad daylight and full voice — a nation glad to be bound, and eager that heaven and earth alike should hear it commit itself to the LORD. There is no shame in the sound and no reluctance in the shout; it is the noise of a people who have found that to be pledged to God is not a bondage but a joy, and who would have all the world know whose they are.
15:
The covenant closes on a note of mutual satisfaction — the people rejoicing, and God found of them — "for they had sworn with all their heart, and sought him with their whole desire; and he was found of them: and the LORD gave them rest round about." The reformed John Gill enters one honest qualification: all Judah rejoiced, that is the greater part of them, for there might be some dissemblers among the throng whose hearts were not in the shout. The rejoicing was real and general, yet Gill will not pretend it was universal.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fastens on the answering mercy. "With their whole desire" he renders "with perfect willingness," the Vulgate's in tota voluntate; and "he was found of them" he reads as the exact discharge of the prophet's promise at v.2, that if ye seek him he will be found of you. The "rest round about" he takes for another period of tranquillity like that already granted at 2 Chron. 14:6-7, and perhaps of equal length. Keil and Delitzsch read the sequence as cause and effect: because they had sworn with their whole heart and sought the LORD with entire willingness and alacrity, therefore Jahve was found of them and gave them rest on every side. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley adds the devotional moral — the times of renewing our covenant with God should be times of rejoicing, for it is an honour and a happiness to be in bonds with God, and the closer the better.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the whole into a maxim of providence. God did well for them: he was found of them and gave them rest round about, so that there was no war for a long time after — national piety, Henry concludes, procures national blessings. The witnesses do not divide. Gill guards the honesty of the joy, Ellicott and Keil show the mercy answering the promise word for word, Wesley draws the sweetness of covenant bonds, Henry the law that binds a people's peace to its piety. Between them they close the covenant scene where it ought to close — with a God who keeps his word to those who keep theirs, meeting a nation's whole-hearted seeking with his own presence and the gift of rest. The reformation begun in a prophet's rebuke ends in a people's gladness and a kingdom's quiet, the visible seal that the LORD is indeed with those who are with him.
16:
The reformation now reaches into the palace itself, for Asa "removed Maachah his mother from being queen, because she had made an idol in a grove," cutting it down, crushing it, and burning it at the brook Kidron. The witnesses agree at once on her identity. The reformed John Gill notes that "mother" means rather grandmother, and the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms it — she was the mother of Abijah who enjoyed the rank of queen-mother through his short reign and on into her grandson Asa's, until deposed for her idolatry. Ellicott firmly rejects the theory that the Maachah who was mother of Abijah and the Maachah who was "mother" of Asa were two different women; there are, he says, no grounds for it.

Ellicott's philology sharpens the scene. "Queen" is gebirah, lady or mistress, always used of a queen, the very rank Athaliah would later usurp at 2 Chron. 22:2; the "idol" is miphletseth, a thing of fear, a horror, a term found only here and in the parallel at 1 Kings 15:13; and "in a grove" is better "for Asherah," the goddess named at 2 Kings 17:16. The word "crushed" he marks as a detail the chronicler adds, recalling how Moses ground the golden calf at Exodus 32:20 and Josiah the high place at Bethel at 2 Kings 23:15.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry praises the courage of the act. It was bravely done of Asa that he would not connive at idolatry in those nearest to him, like Levi who said to father and mother, I have not seen him, at Deut. 33:9; Asa knew he must honour God more than his grandmother, and dared not leave an idol in an apartment of his palace while he was destroying idols in the cities of his kingdom. Maachah, Henry supposes, was so far convinced of her sin as to sign the association, and so was not put to death; yet, because she had been an idolater, Asa thought fit to strip her of her dignity and authority, and probably banished her from court, lest she infect others. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke passes on the Jewish gloss that Maachah repented and had her name changed to Michaiah, daughter of Uriel of Gibeah, that no mention of her former name might reproach her — a legend he reports without endorsing. The witnesses converge: a reforming king spared no rank and no kinship, deposing even the queen-mother that the land might be clean.
17:
A candid qualification follows the reforms: "but the high places were not taken away out of Israel: nevertheless the heart of Asa was perfect all his days." The verse seems to sit awkwardly beside the earlier notice that Asa had removed the high places at 2 Chron. 14:3, 5, and the witnesses work to reconcile the two. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it of a reform thorough in substance but incomplete in detail: Asa had totally suppressed the idolatry, yet permitted some of the places, buildings, or altars to remain standing.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott offers the sharpest solution. The earlier passage, he suggests, relates what the good king resolved and attempted to effect; the present one records his want of success, owing to the obstinate attachment of the people to their old sanctuaries — the same kind of explanation that reconciles the like pair of statements at 2 Chron. 17:6 and 2 Chron. 20:33. He notes that "out of Israel" here means the southern kingdom, a phrase the parallel in Kings lacks, and that where Kings adds "with Jehovah," the sense of the perfect heart is that although Asa failed to be rid of the high places, he himself remained always faithful to the lawful worship of the temple, as David charged Solomon at 1 Chron. 28:9.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the pastoral distinction and the comfort. The reformation was not complete, he grants — the high places were not all taken away, though many were: those in the cities were removed, but perhaps not those in the country, or those used in the worship of false gods were destroyed while those abused in the service of the God of Israel were connived at. Yet Asa's heart was perfect, and here Henry finds his lesson: there may be defects in some particular duties where the heart of a man is nonetheless upright with God, for sincerity is something less than sinless perfection. The witnesses do not finally divide; each softens the seeming contradiction from a different side. Clarke separates the idolatry suppressed from the buildings left, Ellicott the king's resolve from the people's resistance, Henry the false high places purged from the irregular ones tolerated. Between them they secure both halves of the verse — an imperfect reformation and a perfect heart — and let the record stand as an honest one, praising a king who did much without pretending he did all, and grounding his acceptance not in a flawless record but in an undivided love.
18:
Asa's devotion is crowned by a dedication: "he brought into the house of God the things that his father had dedicated, and that he himself had dedicated, silver, and gold, and vessels." The witnesses trace the origin of these consecrated treasures. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reasons that, as it was the custom to dedicate a part of the spoils taken from an enemy to the service and honour of God, Abijah, having so signally overthrown Jeroboam at 2 Chron. 13:15-19, had devoted a portion of that plunder to the LORD, though it had not been brought into the temple until now. The word rendered "vessels," Clarke adds, is kelim, which signifies instruments, utensils, and ornaments of every kind.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms the account and draws a critical inference from it. The verse is identical with its parallel at 1 Kings 15:15, substituting "God" for "Jehovah"; the things Asa's father had dedicated were doubtless taken from the spoils after Abijah's great victory over Jeroboam at 2 Chron. 13:16-19, and the things Asa himself dedicated were a portion of the Cushite booty from 2 Chron. 14:13-15. The brief reference contained in that single verse of Kings is thus, Ellicott argues, an evident confirmation of the chronicler's narrative of the victories of Abijah and Asa, which the chronicler alone records — the older history quietly presupposing the very battles the fuller history relates.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the act as plain honesty toward God. As Asa had taken care that the altar should have its gift, so he took care that the temple should have its gold; and it is honesty, Henry says, to render to God the things that are his. What had been long designed for him, and long laid by for him, as these dedicated things seem to have been, should at length be laid out for him — for will a man rob God, or make slow payment to him who is always ready to do us good? The allusion is to Malachi's charge at Malachi 3:8. The witnesses do not divide. Clarke and Ellicott fix the source of the treasures in the spoils of two victories, Ellicott the confirmation the verse lends to the chronicler's record, Henry the duty of rendering God his due without delay. Between them they show a king who would not let the vows of his house lie unpaid — bringing at last into the temple the gold long owed to God, and so sealing his reformation with an act of belated but wholehearted honesty.
19:
The chapter closes on a note of hard-won peace: "there was no more war unto the five and thirtieth year of the reign of Asa." Two difficulties meet the witnesses here — how this squares with the statement in Kings that war ran between Asa and Baasha all their days, and what to make of the puzzling date. The reformed John Gill resolves the first by distinguishing open war from low-grade hostility: from the Ethiopian war onward there was no war with any foreign enemy, though there were animosities, discords, and bickerings of some sort continually between Asa and Baasha as long as he lived. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads it the same way, noting that both 1 Kings 15:16 and this verse begin with the same two Hebrew words, "and war was," save that the chronicler inserts a "not"; the verse of Kings need imply no more than that no amicable relations were ever established, the two kings having inherited a state of war though neither could yet make an open attack. Keil and Delitzsch concur, taking the "war" of Kings to denote the latent hostility of the two kingdoms, so that the "no war" of the Chronicle refers to actual armed conflict.

The date itself divides them. Ellicott confesses the "five and thirtieth year" does not agree with the data of Kings, and relays the conjecture of Thenius that a copyist's error inflated the figure — the letter for thirty having crept in by dittography — so that the original readings were the fifth and sixth years, the false dates already present in the source the chronicler followed. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke offers two other escapes: Archbishop Usher would count the thirty-five years from the division of the kingdom, which brings the date to the fifteenth year of Asa's reign; or, Clarke suspects, we should simply read here "the five and twentieth year." He adds a rueful confession that to settle these chronologies is a most difficult undertaking, in which the sacred books stand in no worse case than every other ancient record.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry passes lightly over the arithmetic to the mercy the verse records: there was no war for a long time after, no open general war, though there were constant frontier skirmishes between Judah and Israel. The witnesses, then, agree on the substance — a long reprieve of peace, the fruit of the covenant just sworn — while dividing over the number. Gill, Ellicott, and Keil harmonize the "no war" with the standing enmity of Kings; Clarke and Ellicott, with Usher and Thenius, wrestle the stubborn date. Between them they let the chapter end where the covenant pointed, in rest — a rest real though not unbroken, granted to a people that had sought the LORD with its whole heart.
